claims.text: The starting material is an as-cast, single-phase Ti-Ni-containing high-entropy alloy in a solid-solution state.
Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 is presented as an example alloy having Ni as a primary or major constituent.
The proposed aging treatment is 650–750 °C for 10–60 minutes followed by rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching after aging will retain a fine precipitate distribution.
The aging treatment will form uniformly distributed, coherent nanoscale Ni3Ti precipitates.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates can strengthen an HEA matrix by obstructing dislocation motion.
Ni3Ti precipitates will pin dislocations during high-temperature deformation.
Precipitation hardening from the proposed Ni3Ti dispersion will increase elevated-temperature tensile yield strength.
Precipitation hardening from the proposed Ni3Ti dispersion will improve elevated-temperature creep resistance.
The intervention is applicable to equiatomic or near-equiatomic Ti-Ni-containing HEAs initially processed as single-phase solid solutions.
The relevant tensile and creep test regime extends to approximately 800–900 °C.
The refractory Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy has previously been mechanically tested at elevated temperatures including 800 °C.
High-temperature aging may produce detrimental alpha-Ti precipitates.
Extended high-temperature exposure may coarsen the proposed Ni3Ti precipitates.
A lack of at least approximately 10% improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength or creep resistance relative to an untreated same-batch control is a proposed falsification criterion.
Failure to detect uniformly distributed, coherent nanoscale Ni3Ti precipitates by microscopy is a proposed falsification criterion.

contradictions.description: The material is repeatedly described as having Ni as a primary or major constituent, but the only explicit example, Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20, contains no Ni. Ni3Ti precipitation is therefore chemically impossible in the stated example.
